title: Explain Common Features and Tools of the macOS/Desktop Operating System

sections.title: What You Are Learning
paragraphs: macOS uses distinct application formats, folders, security features, navigation tools, backup services, cloud services, and utilities.
The main mental model is: install → navigate → configure → protect → back up → troubleshoot.

sections.title: Maestro Focus
paragraphs: When a Mac scenario describes installing software, locating files, configuring settings, protecting data, using cloud services, or troubleshooting, can you select the correct feature or tool?

entries.title: File Types
paragraphs: macOS software commonly arrives as disk images, installer packages, or application bundles.

entries.title: .dmg
paragraphs: A disk image mounts like a virtual disk and commonly contains an application, installer, or instructions. A common flow is open the .dmg, drag the .app into Applications, then eject the image.

entries.title: .pkg
paragraphs: An installer package runs an installation workflow and can place components in required system locations.

entries.title: .app
paragraphs: An application bundle appears as one program even though it contains multiple internal files.

entries.title: App Store
paragraphs: The App Store supplies Apple-managed application distribution, installation, updates, and Apple ID integration.

entries.title: Uninstallation Process
paragraphs: Many apps can be removed from Applications, but complex apps may include an uninstaller or leave support files. Do not assume deleting one icon always removes everything.

table.caption: Important macOS paths
rows: Support data and settings for one user

sections.title: Apple ID and Corporate Restrictions
paragraphs: An Apple ID provides access to iCloud, the App Store, iMessage, FaceTime, and other Apple services. Organization-managed Macs may restrict applications, settings, accounts, security features, or cloud services.
sections.callout: A setting disabled by company management → corporate restriction or policy.

entries.title: Backups
paragraphs: Backups protect against failure, deletion, corruption, and loss. Time Machine is the built-in macOS backup system.

entries.title: Antivirus
paragraphs: Macs are not immune to malware; endpoint protection may be appropriate for the risk and organizational requirements.

entries.title: Updates/Patches
paragraphs: OS and application updates deliver security, stability, compatibility, and bug fixes.

entries.title: Rapid Security Response (RSR)
paragraphs: RSR lets Apple deliver urgent security improvements without waiting for a full traditional OS update.
entries.recognitionCue: Urgent Apple security fix outside a major update → RSR.

sections.title: System Preferences
paragraphs: Depending on the macOS version, Apple uses the names System Preferences or System Settings.

entries.title: Displays
paragraphs: Controls resolution, arrangement, brightness, and external displays.

entries.title: Networks
paragraphs: Configures Wi-Fi, Ethernet, and other interfaces.

entries.title: Printers
paragraphs: Adds, removes, and manages printers.

entries.title: Scanners
paragraphs: Adds, removes, and manages scanners.

entries.title: Privacy
paragraphs: Controls application access to camera, microphone, location, files, and other protected resources.

entries.title: Accessibility
paragraphs: Provides assistive visual, hearing, motor, and interaction features.

entries.title: Time Machine
paragraphs: Configures macOS backup destinations and historical file recovery.

entries.title: Multiple Desktops
paragraphs: Virtual desktops, called Spaces, separate workspaces.

entries.title: Mission Control
paragraphs: Shows an overview of open windows, full-screen applications, and Spaces.
entries.recognitionCue: See all workspaces and windows → Mission Control.

entries.title: Keychain
paragraphs: Stores passwords, certificates, and cryptographic keys.
entries.recognitionCue: Inspect a saved password or certificate → Keychain.

entries.title: Spotlight
paragraphs: Searches applications, files, and information on the Mac.

entries.title: Gestures
paragraphs: Multi-finger trackpad and pointing-device actions scroll, zoom, switch Spaces, and open Mission Control.

entries.title: Finder
paragraphs: Finder is the macOS file manager for browsing and managing files and folders.

entries.title: Dock
paragraphs: The Dock launches and switches applications and provides access to selected files, folders, running apps, and Trash.

entries.title: Continuity
paragraphs: Continuity connects supported Apple devices so a workflow can start on one device and continue on another.

sections.title: iCloud

entries.title: iMessage
paragraphs: Apple's messaging service.

entries.title: FaceTime
paragraphs: Apple's audio and video calling service.

entries.title: Drive
paragraphs: iCloud Drive stores and synchronizes files through Apple's cloud service.

sections.callout: Time Machine is backup and recovery; iCloud Drive is cloud storage and synchronization.

sections.title: Disk Utility
paragraphs: Disk Utility manages storage devices and volumes, formatting, partitions, and supported disk checking or repair operations.
sections.callout: Mac disks and volumes → Disk Utility.

sections.title: FileVault
paragraphs: FileVault provides full-disk encryption to protect stored Mac data if the device is lost or stolen.

sections.title: Terminal
paragraphs: Terminal provides command-line access to macOS.

sections.title: Force Quit
paragraphs: Force Quit closes an unresponsive application when normal Quit fails. It is available from the Apple menu and a keyboard shortcut.

entries.title: .dmg vs. .pkg vs. .app
paragraphs: .dmg is a container, .pkg is an installer, and .app is the application bundle.

entries.title: /Library vs. User Library
paragraphs: /Library is system-wide; ~/Library belongs to one user.

entries.title: Finder vs. Spotlight
paragraphs: Finder browses and manages files; Spotlight searches.

entries.title: Mission Control vs. Multiple Desktops
paragraphs: Multiple desktops are workspaces; Mission Control shows and manages them.

entries.title: Keychain vs. FileVault
paragraphs: Keychain stores credentials; FileVault encrypts the disk.

entries.title: Time Machine vs. iCloud Drive
paragraphs: Time Machine is backup and recovery; iCloud Drive is cloud synchronization.

entries.title: Disk Utility vs. Finder
paragraphs: Disk Utility manages devices and volumes; Finder manages files and folders.
